objective: Implementing interface management: planning interface points (IPs) across packages, classifying interfaces on mega projects, and applying industry-leading frameworks

sources.cite: PMI, PMI Construction Professional (PMI-CP) Examination Content Outline (February 2024): Contracts Management 50%, Stakeholder Engagement 30%, Strategy and Scope Management 15%, Project Governance 5%
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of a copy hosted on Scribd: the domain weights only; the task text was not shown. The objective wording is the course seed's, built from PMI's outline read on 2026-09-27 (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/pm.ts); the claims task text is to verify against PMI's PDF. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's clinic-fitout-claim-pmicp (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The organization, the project, the figures and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You manage interfaces on a fictional light-rail depot for Tidewater Transit, split into five contract packages: civil, track, systems, buildings and power.
handover: The civil contractor poured a slab last week without the power package's duct banks.
There is no interface register; issues surface on site.
howItWorks: The dashboard shows the commitments, the work items, the risks and issues, the people's support and the milestones.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each status meeting; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

clash.available: not busy and phase == "run" and isNull(clashAt)
clash.why: Done, or finish what you are doing first.

effects.finding: Power duct banks were missing from civil's drawings; breaking out and recasting costs 140 thousand dollars and 3 weeks.

scopes.label: Compare the five package scopes
scopes.available: not busy and phase == "run" and isNull(scopesAt)
scopes.why: Done, or finish what you are doing first.

effects.finding: At least 40 physical and functional handovers between packages are named in no contract.

options.label: An interface register with owners, interfaces classified with weekly review of critical points, and the rework settled with need dates added

then.log: Week 2: the track contractor installs rails over a systems cable route; another break-out is needed.
Week 3: nobody owns the integrated signal test between systems and track; commissioning stalls.
Week 4: a similar data gap on the buildings package costs another 90 thousand dollars from contingency.

choices.label: Build an interface register: each interface point with the two packages, the giving and receiving party, data needed, a need date and an owner, agreed at a joint workshop

effects.log: Forty interface points are registered and agreed.

choices.feedback: Interface management plans each interface point between packages with owners and need dates.

choices.label: Discuss interfaces at the weekly site meeting as they come up

effects.log: A standing agenda item is added.

choices.feedback: Issues are found when they hit the site, as the slab was.

choices.label: Tell contractors to coordinate among themselves
choices.feedback: Nobody owns the gaps; each contractor protects its own scope.

classifyPrompt.title: Which interfaces need the most attention
classifyPrompt.context: Forty points cannot all get equal attention.

choices.label: Classify each point as physical, functional, contractual or organizational, and by criticality to the schedule, reviewing critical ones weekly

effects.log: Twelve critical points get weekly review.

choices.feedback: On large projects, interfaces are classified so critical ones get the closest control.

choices.label: Review all 40 equally every month
choices.feedback: Critical handovers wait a month for attention.

choices.label: Track only physical clashes; drop the rest
choices.feedback: Functional and contractual gaps, such as test responsibilities, are lost.

changePrompt.title: The duct bank rework
changePrompt.context: Civil says power's data was late; power says civil never asked.

choices.label: Treat the rework as a change under the contracts, determine responsibility from the record, and add a data-exchange need date to every related interface point

effects.log: The change is settled; need dates are added.

choices.feedback: Interface failures are settled through contract mechanisms, and the register is updated so the gap does not recur.

choices.label: Split the cost evenly between the two contractors
choices.feedback: Quick, but not based on the record and it teaches nothing.

choices.label: Pay it from the owner's contingency and say nothing
choices.feedback: The cause stays unfixed and contingency shrinks.

reflection.question: Write the interface record for the owner's director.

parts.label: Register
parts.criteria: 40 interface points with owners and need dates; 12 critical reviewed weekly.
parts.modelAnswer: Every handover between the five packages is registered with giving and receiving parties, data needs, need dates and owners; 12 critical points are reviewed weekly.

parts.label: The slab
parts.criteria: Settled under the contracts; need dates added.
parts.modelAnswer: The duct bank rework was settled under the contracts from the record, and every related interface now has a data-exchange need date.

scoring.modelReasoning: Interface management plans every interface point between contract packages, with giving and receiving parties, data needs, need dates and owners. Classify interfaces by type and criticality so the critical ones get close control, and settle interface failures through the contracts while feeding the lessons back into the register.
